## Common Collocations
- **pagar en efectivo** — to pay in cash; "en efectivo," not "con efectivo"
- **pagar con tarjeta** — to pay by card; "con tarjeta," not "por tarjeta"
- **estar de oferta / estar en rebaja** — to be on sale
- **ir de compras** — to go shopping; uses **de**, not "a" or "para"
- **hacer fila / hacer cola** — to stand in line; literally "to make a line"
- **cobrar de más** — to overcharge
- **¿A cuánto está(n)?** — How much is it / are they?; common market phrasing
- **¿Cuánto cuesta?** — How much does it cost?; standard question
- **No me queda** — It doesn't fit me (clothing); literally "it doesn't remain on me"
- **quedar bien/mal** — to fit well/poorly; "La camisa me queda grande" (the shirt is too big on me)

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **la ropa** vs **rope**: **Ropa** means "clothing." Rope is **la cuerda**.
- **la marca** vs **mark**: **Marca** means "brand." A mark/grade is **la nota** or **la marca** (context-dependent).
- **efectivo** vs **effective**: As a noun, **el efectivo** means "cash." As an adjective, it does mean "effective."
- **probar** vs **prove**: **Probar** means "to try" or "to taste." To prove is **demostrar** or **comprobar**.
- **actual** vs **actual**: **Actual** means "current." Actual is **real** or **verdadero**. "El precio actual" = the current price.

## Dialect Variations
- **money**: **el dinero** (universal/formal), **la plata** (Argentina, Colombia, Chile, Peru — colloquial), **la lana** (Mexico — slang)
- **line/queue**: **la fila** (Latin America), **la cola** (Spain). Both widely understood.
- **bag**: **la bolsa** (universal), **la funda** (Ecuador), **la jaba** (Cuba)
- **receipt**: **el recibo** (universal), **el ticket** (informal, from English, common in Latin America), **la boleta** (Chile, Peru)
- **wallet**: **la cartera** (Mexico — wallet; Spain/South America — purse), **la billetera** (South America — wallet)
- **cheap**: **barato** (universal), **chafa** (Mexico — slang for cheap/low quality)

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Bargaining (regatear)**: In traditional markets (mercados) and street vendors, bargaining is expected and part of the social interaction. In stores, supermarkets, and malls, prices are fixed — attempting to bargain is awkward. A polite opener: "¿Me puede hacer un descuento?" or "¿Cuál es su mejor precio?"
- **Cash culture**: Many small shops and markets in Latin America are cash-only or offer discounts for cash payment. "¿Tiene descuento si pago en efectivo?" is a common question.
- **Shopping small talk**: Vendors in markets often greet with "¿Qué va a llevar?" (What are you going to take?) or "¿Le puedo ayudar?" Responding with "Solo estoy viendo" (I'm just looking) is polite.
- **Tipping**: In Latin America, grocery store baggers (empacadores) are often unpaid volunteers who work for tips. A small tip is customary.
- **"Le queda bien"**: Salespeople frequently use this phrase (It looks good on you / It fits you well) as encouragement. Knowing **quedar** in this context helps navigate shopping conversations.
- **Direct object pronouns in shopping**: Shopping is a natural context for direct object pronoun practice. "¿Tiene la camisa en azul?" → "Sí, **la** tengo." "¿Quiere estos zapatos?" → "Sí, **los** quiero." This reinforces B-06.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **precio** — the **ci** combination: PRE-sio (not "pre-see-oh" with a hard English 's'). The c before i is /s/ in Latin America, /θ/ in Spain.
- **regatear** — four syllables: re-ga-te-AR. Stress on last syllable. The **g** is a soft /ɡ/ between vowels.
- **efectivo** — stress on penultimate: e-fec-TI-vo. Not "effective" with English stress pattern.
- **descuento** — the **ue** diphthong: des-CUEN-to. Both vowels in the diphthong must be pronounced.
- **rebaja** — the **j** is the Spanish /x/ (guttural h): re-BA-ja. Not a French "zh" sound.
- **cambio** — two syllables, not three: CAM-bio. The **io** is a diphthong.
